citation: Stamatatos, E. (2009). A survey of modern authorship attribution methods. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 60(3), 538–556.
claim_support: Survey of text representations, classifiers, computational settings and evaluation in authorship attribution. Supports dependence of attribution evidence on the representation and evaluation design.
evidence: Publisher abstract and article metadata inspected; author-hosted full-text copy also indexed.

citation: Burrows, J. (2002). ‘Delta’: A measure of stylistic difference and a guide to likely authorship. Literary and Linguistic Computing, 17(3), 267–287.
claim_support: Origin of Delta using standardized frequent-word profiles for stylistic comparison and attribution. Does not justify calling Euclidean nearest centroid the Burrows Delta algorithm.
evidence: Publisher-deposited Crossref metadata checked; technical content cross-checked against Argamon (2008) and the publisher's current Delta application.

citation: Argamon, S. (2008). Interpreting Burrows’s Delta: Geometric and probabilistic foundations. Literary and Linguistic Computing, 23(2), 131–147.
claim_support: Interprets Delta geometrically and probabilistically, clarifying assumptions, limitations and variants. Appropriate background for interpreting feature geometry; not a prior result for the present affine rewrite model.
evidence: Official Oxford article abstract and volume/issue metadata inspected. Use issue year 2008; Crossref online-date field was inconsistent with the publisher page.

citation: Sapkota, U., Bethard, S., Montes, M., & Solorio, T. (2015). Not all character n-grams are created equal: A study in authorship attribution. In Proceedings of the 2015 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (pp. 93–102). Association for Computational Linguistics.
claim_support: Character n-grams mix affix, word and punctuation information; categories differ in contribution to attribution. Supports caution that predictive character features are not uniformly content-independent.
evidence: ACL bibliographic page and primary PDF sections 1–2 inspected. ACL uses author name Manuel Montes, while some indexing sites expand it to Montes-y-Gómez.

citation: Stamatatos, E. (2017). Authorship attribution using text distortion. In Proceedings of the 15th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Volume 1, Long Papers (pp. 1138–1149). Association for Computational Linguistics.
claim_support: Text distortion masks topic-specific information and improves cross-topic attribution in evaluated settings. Supports topic controls, not a claim that function words eliminate every content confound.
evidence: ACL abstract, metadata and author-hosted PDF inspected. ACL page gives no DOI, so none is invented.

citation: Kestemont, M. (2014). Function words in authorship attribution. From black magic to theory? In Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Computational Linguistics for Literature (CLFL) (pp. 59–66). Association for Computational Linguistics.
claim_support: Theoretical discussion of function-word features and methodological assumptions in stylometry; supports using interpretable linguistic representations without treating function words as infallible author markers.
evidence: ACL page, PDF and publisher-deposited Crossref metadata inspected.

citation: Sundararajan, K., & Woodard, D. (2018). What represents ‘style’ in authorship attribution? In Proceedings of the 27th International Conference on Computational Linguistics (pp. 2814–2822). Association for Computational Linguistics.
claim_support: Investigates syntax and lexical features across topic and genre. Finds topic interference and representation-dependent cross-domain behavior; does not support universal topic independence for one feature family.
evidence: ACL bibliographic page and PDF abstract/introduction inspected. PDF heading says ‘What constitutes’; official ACL title is retained consistently here.

citation: Eder, M. (2015). Does size matter? Authorship attribution, small samples, big problem. Digital Scholarship in the Humanities, 30(2), 167–182.
claim_support: Examines stability of attribution with varying sample length, language, genre and sampling. Supports length sensitivity and caution with short passages; its corpus-specific thresholds are not universal requirements.
evidence: Publisher-deposited Crossref title, authors, pages and print date checked: print June 2015, advance online November 2013. Primary paper PDF available through university teaching materials.

citation: Covington, M. A., & McFall, J. D. (2010). Cutting the Gordian knot: The moving-average type–token ratio (MATTR). Journal of Quantitative Linguistics, 17(2), 94–100.
claim_support: Introduces moving-window type–token ratio to address ordinary TTR's dependence on text length. Background only: do not claim this study computed MATTR unless code confirms it.
evidence: Official publisher abstract and Crossref bibliographic metadata inspected.

citation: Tripto, N. I., Venkatraman, S., Macko, D., Moro, R., Srba, I., Uchendu, A., Le, T., & Lee, D. (2024). A ship of Theseus: Curious cases of paraphrasing in LLM-generated texts. In Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers) (pp. 6608–6625). Association for Computational Linguistics.
claim_support: Repeated paraphrasing is associated with changes in source style and decreasing classification performance. Establishes that paraphrase-induced attribution change predates the current study.
evidence: ACL abstract and full bibliographic metadata inspected. Claims here are restricted to the documented iterative-paraphrasing design and abstract findings.

citation: Fisher, J., Lu, X., Jung, J., Jiang, L., Harchaoui, Z., & Choi, Y. (2024). JAMDEC: Unsupervised authorship obfuscation using constrained decoding over small language models. In Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers) (pp. 1552–1581). Association for Computational Linguistics.
claim_support: Inference-time authorship obfuscation with constrained decoding, small language models and content/fluency preservation. Its objective is deliberate obfuscation, unlike generic modernization or simplification.
evidence: ACL abstract and full bibliographic metadata inspected.

citation: Fisher, J., Hallinan, S., Lu, X., Gordon, M. L., Harchaoui, Z., & Choi, Y. (2024). StyleRemix: Interpretable authorship obfuscation via distillation and perturbation of style elements. In Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (pp. 4172–4206). Association for Computational Linguistics.
claim_support: Targeted perturbation of style dimensions for authorship obfuscation, with automatic and human evaluation. Controls and interpretability in rewriting are prior work, not new merely because more deployment labels are tested.
evidence: ACL abstract and full bibliographic metadata inspected.

citation: Malik, U., & Awan, M. S. (2026). The assistant erased you: Measuring loss of authorship signals in AI-mediated communication. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.00926
claim_support: Defines Idiolect Erasure Rate as the drop in attribution accuracy after rewriting; tests blogs, email and news with stylometric and LUAR attribution. Method sections 3.1–3.2 use original-trained attributers on held-out messages and light/heavy/voice-preserving prompts. This is close prior work for paired attribution loss; current distinctions must concern work holdouts, retraining, held-out affine prediction and explicit semantic/failure accounting.
evidence: Primary arXiv abstract and full-text sections 1–3 read at https://arxiv.org/html/2608.00926v1. v1 submitted 2026-08-02. No peer-reviewed venue asserted.

citation: Thejaswi, S., Kulshreshta, J., & Oettershagen, L. (2026). Linguistic monoculture in LLM-assisted language use. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2607.27134
claim_support: Mathematical model of author/LLM distributions evolving through repeated interaction, with shared, recursive and personalized mechanisms; studies equilibria, convergence and synthetic simulations. Rules out claiming mathematical homogenization is unexplored. The present empirical single-rewrite centroid regression addresses a different quantity and does not estimate long-run author adaptation.
evidence: Primary arXiv metadata and full-text introduction, stated mechanisms and theoretical sections inspected at https://arxiv.org/html/2607.27134v1. Author spelling follows arXiv: Kulshreshta. v1 submitted 2026-07-29. No peer-reviewed venue asserted.

citation: Fitterer, S., Gangl, D., & Ulbrich, J. (2025). Testing English news articles for lexical homogenization due to widespread use of large language models. In Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 4: Student Research Workshop) (pp. 1239–1245). Association for Computational Linguistics.
claim_support: Compares 2018 and 2024 news corpora; selected diversity measures do not show the hypothesized lexical homogenization uniformly. Useful counterexample to universal linguistic convergence claims; observational news comparison differs from paired rewriting.
evidence: ACL abstract and complete bibliographic metadata inspected.

citation: Mikros, G., Sosoni, V., Manousakis, V., & Polychroniou, K. (2026). Burrows’ Delta as a convergent validator: Stylometric analysis for complementary machine translation evaluation. Journal of Quantitative Linguistics. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1080/09296174.2026.2612931
claim_support: Uses stylometry as complementary evidence for machine-translation evaluation, with distinct adequacy-oriented metrics; argues against interpreting style distance as a complete substitute for meaning evaluation. The one-author-translator Greek/English design is not the current six-author intralingual rewriting design.
evidence: Publisher-indexed full article sections 4, 6, 8.3 and data statement inspected; Crossref authors/title/DOI checked, online date 2026-02-10, currently no volume/issue, article pages 1–29.

citation: Ben-David, S., Blitzer, J., Crammer, K., Kulesza, A., Pereira, F., & Vaughan, J. W. (2010). A theory of learning from different domains. Machine Learning, 79(1–2), 151–175.
claim_support: Theory of source/target distribution mismatch and target-domain performance. Conceptual background for domain transfer; the present arithmetic macro-F1 decomposition is not derived as one of this paper's bounds.
evidence: Official Springer abstract, author list and issue-year metadata inspected.

citation: Gries, S. Th. (2022). Toward more careful corpus statistics: Uncertainty estimates for frequencies, dispersions, association measures, and more. Research Methods in Applied Linguistics, 1(1), 100002.
claim_support: Advocates text/file-based bootstrap uncertainty for corpus statistics instead of treating all tokens as exchangeable. Supports clustered analysis logic, not the assertion that the present conditional bootstrap captures training uncertainty.
evidence: Official publisher abstract, author-hosted full-text excerpt and Crossref metadata inspected.

citation: Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 6(2), 65–70.
claim_support: Sequential Bonferroni/Holm multiple-test procedure for familywise error control. Appropriate citation for a common correction across the 54 primary tests.
evidence: Primary journal scan title, author, volume, issue and pages inspected at https://www.ime.usp.br/~abe/lista/pdf4R8xPVzCnX.pdf. JSTOR identifier is supplied; Crossref endpoint did not return a work record in this audit.

citation: Ledoit, O., & Wolf, M. (2004). A well-conditioned estimator for large-dimensional covariance matrices. Journal of Multivariate Analysis, 88(2), 365–411.
claim_support: Shrinkage covariance estimation for conditioning and accuracy in large dimensions. Supports the covariance-shrinkage motivation; exact LDA implementation must still be documented from code.
evidence: Publisher abstract and author-hosted primary PDF inspected.

citation: Artstein, R., & Poesio, M. (2008). Inter-coder agreement for computational linguistics. Computational Linguistics, 34(4), 555–596.
claim_support: Discusses agreement measures and assumptions for computational annotation. Relevant to reporting actual rater structure and distinguishing agreement from correctness or independence.
evidence: ACL metadata and full-text discussion of replicability and arbitration inspected. Bibliographic title sometimes includes the article-type prefix ‘Survey Article:’; that prefix is omitted consistently here.
